title: Detection of a Rare Intra-ALK Inversion and ALK Rearrangement in a Lung Adenocarcinoma Patient by FoundationOne Liquid CDx and Successful Treatment with Alectinib: Case Report
author: Chiaki Kanno; Satoshi Takahashi; Masaru Hagiwara; Hideyuki Furumoto; Yujin Kudo; Yoshihisa Shimada; Masatoshi Kakihana; Tatsuo Ohira; Norihiko Ikeda
text:
Abstract
A 50-year-old woman with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma tested negative for driver mutations using the Oncomine Dx Target Test Multi-CDx system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). After undergoing chemotherapy and immunotherapy, FoundationOne Liquid CDx (Foundation Medicine, Inc., Cambridge, MA) identified a rare EML4-ALK gene rearrangement. Treatment with alectinib led to rapid clinical improvement and sustained disease control for more than 7 months. This case highlights the value of next-generation sequencing-based profiling in detecting rare actionable alterations missed by standard tests. We also include a discussion on why the EML4-AKL fusion was not detected in the usual test.
Keywords: Non–small cell lung cancer, ALK-EML4 rearrangement, FoundationOne Liquid CDx, Comprehensive genome profiling, Case report
Introduction
The EML4-ALK fusion gene, first described in 2007, is a well-known driver mutation found in approximately 2% to 5% of NSCLCs.1 The development of ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) has markedly improved the outcomes of patients with NSCLC who have these mutations.2
The detection of gene mutations is typically performed using companion diagnostics, such as Oncomine CDx (Thermo Fisher Scientific); however, rare or atypical gene fusions may not be detected by these conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–based assays. In recent years, next-generation sequencing has become an essential tool in precision oncology, enabling comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) and the identification of rare but actionable gene alterations.
Here, we report a case of a patient with advanced NSCLC, in whom a rare EML4-ALK rearrangement, undetected by standard testing, was successfully identified through next-generation sequencing-based FoundationOne Liquid CDx (Foundation Medicine, Inc.). The patient exhibited a remarkable clinical response to alectinib after experiencing rapid disease progression while undergoing multiple systemic therapies, including treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).
Case Presentation
A 50-year-old nonsmoking woman without notable symptoms was referred to our hospital after an abnormal shadow was noted during a medical check-up. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a solid 2.4-cm nodule in the right lower lobe, S6 area. Enlarged ipsilateral hilar, mediastinal, and supraclavicular lymph nodes were also observed (Fig. 1A–B). On 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography–CT, substantial FDG uptake was observed, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 11 in the primary lesion. Additional uptake was noted in the liver and in the T12 and L3 vertebrae (Fig. 1C–F). Her serum carcinoembryonic antigen level was elevated to 149 ng/mL. Histopathologic analysis confirmed adenocarcinoma, and she was diagnosed as having stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma (cT1cN3M1c, eighth Union for International Cancer Control). Molecular testing using the Oncomine Dx Target Test (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was unable to detect any actionable gene mutation, and programmed cell death ligand 1 expression (22C3 assay) was found to be less than 1% (tumor proportion score).
First-line chemotherapy comprising cisplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab was initiated. After four cycles, CT revealed a partial response, and the patient continued with maintenance therapy (pemetrexed + pembrolizumab). However, 3 months after its initiation, CT revealed the progression of liver metastases. The patient subsequently received second-line docetaxel and ramucirumab, but with limited effect. At this time, she was enrolled in CGP using FoundationOne Liquid CDx and started third-line chemoimmunotherapy while awaiting results. However, the patient developed low-grade fever, abdominal pain, and liver dysfunction with rapid progression of liver metastases. She was emergently hospitalized (Fig. 2A–B).
During the patient’s hospitalization, a rare ALK gene fusion was identified by CGP consisting of two atypical patterns, namely, an inversion of ALK exons 16 to 19, and the ALK-EML4 rearrangement, from ALK exons 1 to 19 to a truncated EML4 region, enabling ALK-targeted therapy. Although these gene patterns did not clearly indicate a functional EML4-ALK fusion, the findings suggested the possible presence of an EML4-ALK chimeric fusion protein in the patient’s tumor cells (Fig. 3A–B). ALK immunohistochemistry testing was also performed, confirming a positive result (Fig. 3C–D). She was a candidate for ALK-targeted therapy. Oral alectinib administration (600 mg/day) was initiated, resulting in rapid clinical improvement. She was discharged within 2 weeks without any notable adverse events.
After 6 months of initiating alectinib treatment, CT imaging revealed marked regression of the liver metastases (Fig. 2C–F), with a decrease in her serum level. At the latest follow-up (about 7 months after starting alectinib treatment), the patient remains on alectinib without any disease progression or notable signs of toxicity (Fig. 4).
Discussion
In this patient, no actionable gene mutations were identified in her tissue using the Oncomine Dx Target Test before treatment. However, two rare ALK gene fusions were identified by FoundationOne Liquid CDx, enabling ALK-targeted therapy.3,4 ALK rearrangement, such as observed here, those that are detected as a reciprocal fusion, are not clearly in frame, may lack a fusion partner, or may lack a partner with oligomerization activity, may be indicative of an activating rearrangement event such as an oncogenic fusion (e.g., EML4-ALK). However, it is unclear whether such rearrangements would lead to oncogenic ALK fusion. On the basis of this possibility and previous in vivo evidence of TKI sensitivity in similar patients, ALK TKI therapy was recommended for this patient. This highlights the need for a broader range of detection strategies beyond conventional PCR-based fusion assays when rare or complex rearrangements are suspected. In recent years, multiplex genetic testing has often been used before initial treatment. However, even when such tests yield negative results, additional ALK immunohistochemistry may be considered in cases with strong clinical suspicion, such as younger, never-smoking patients, because of its high sensitivity and specificity. In this case, the evaluation of multiple genes was required; CGP was performed.
CGP was performed before the patient’s condition deteriorated, enabling the timely initiation of alectinib; however, only 1 month after the last administration of ICI. Although initiating TKI therapy within 3 to 4 months after ICI administration has been associated with an increased risk of adverse events,5 the rapid disease progression of this patient justified the immediate initiation of TKI treatment. Fortunately, TKI responded well without any major complications.
Furthermore, although TP53 gene mutations generally predict a poor response to ALK TKIs, our patient with a TP53 (K120fs) mutation and a rare ALK rearrangement responded well to alectinib.6 This suggests that ALK variant type may affect treatment efficacy, warranting further study.
In conclusion, a rare ALK-EML4 rearrangement in an NSCLC patient that was not detected by conventional PCR-based assays was identified through CGP using Liquid CDx, leading to successful treatment using ALK TKI. Some ALK gene fusion types may evade routine testing, resulting in false negatives. Our case suggests that, in patients with limited options, re-evaluation with CGP may identify actionable mutations and open new treatment paths.
